Whether or not a resolution may amend, modii" or supersede an ordinance; and Whether or not the majority of the members of the City Council have the power to decide how to disburse the MOOE budget job orders, thereby setting aside the authority of the Vice Mayor to appoint officials and employees of the Sanggunian. facts: 2. 3. Based on the documents forwarded to this Department, hereunder are the relevant On 13 September 2016, Resolution No. 292 was adopted by the Sangguniang Panlungsod of Manila assigning five (5) job orders to all SP Members and an additional ten (10) to those SP Members with Standing Committee chairmanships. Vice Mayor Maria Sheilah H. Lacuna asserted that she has the sole authority to appoint all officials of the SangguniangPanlungsod and that power includes the power of assignment. Thereby, refuses to sign Resolution No. 292. On the other hand, Lhe Majority Floor Leader, SP Member Casimiro C. Sison alleges that the power to decide how to disburse the MOOE budget of job orders rests with the majority members of the Sangguniang Panlungsod by virtue of Resolution No. 292. Hence, your subject letter. In order to answer the first issue, we find it is imperative to distinguish an ordinance from a resolution, which are both products of our local legislative bodies such as the local

sanggunians. In the case of Municipality of Paranaque vs. V.M. Realty Corporation', the Supreme Court distinguished the two (2) in this manner: A municipal ordinance is different from a resolution. An ordinance is a law, but a resolution is merely a declaration of the sentiment or opinion of a lawmaking body on specific matter. An ordinance possesses a general and permanent character, but a resolution is temporary in nattlre. Additionally, the two are enacted differently — a third reading is necewsary for an ordinance, but not for a resolution, unless decided otherwise by a majority of all the Sanggunian members. Thus, it is our view that a resolution may not amend, modify or supersede an ordinance. However, in Favis vs. The City of Baguio, et al.2, the Supreme Court held that even if the measure is denominated as a resolution if it is passed in the manner and with the statutory formality required in the enactment of an ordinance, it will be binding and effective as an ordinance. As to the second issue, may we invite your attention to the case of Atienza vs. Villarosa3. In this case, Governor Jose Villarosa of the Province of Occidental Mindoro issued a Memorandum dated 25 June 2002 entitled "AU'ITIORITY TO SIGN PURCHASE ORDERS OF SUPPLIES, MATERIALS, EQUIPMENT(S), INCLUDING FUEL, REPAIRS AND MAINTENANCE OF THE SANGGUNIANG PANLALAWIGAN" stating that all Purchase Orders issued in connection with the procurement of supplies, materials and equipment[sl including fuel, repairs and maintenance needed in the transaction of public business or in the pursuit of any undertaking, project or activity of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan shall be approved by him in his capacity as the local chief executive of the province. Vice-Governor Ramon Atienza replied saying that purchase orders for supplies, materials and equipment are included under those as authorized for signature by the Vice- chief executive of the Sanggunian. For this, Governor Villarosa issued a Memorandum dated 01 July 2002 relating to the 'TERMINATION OF CONTRACT OF SERVICES OF CASUALJJOB ORDER EMPLOYEES AND REAPPOINTMENT OF THE RESPECTIVE RECOMMENDEES." The said memorandum reads: For faithful and appropriate enforcement and execution of laws and issuances and to promote efficiency in the government service, effective immediately, all existing contract of employment — casual/job order basis and reappointment of the recommendees — entered into by Vice-Governor Ramon M. Atienza are hereby terminated for being unauthorized. Aside from being signed by the unauthorized signatory, the following facts regarding the appointments were considered: G.R. In his letter dated 09 July 2002, Vice-Governor Atienza invoked the principle of separation of powers as applied to the local government units. 'l'he request, however, went unheeded as Governor Villarosa insisted on obliging the department heads of the provincial government to comply with the memoranda. The Supreme Court summarized the issues as follows: Who between the petitioner and the respondent is authorized 1. to approve purchase orders issued in connection with the procurement of supplies, materials, equipment, including fuel, repairs and maintenance of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan? Does respondent Villarosa, as local chief executive, have the 2. authority to terminate or cancel the appointments of casual/job order employees of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan Members and the Office of the Vice-Governor? The Supreme Court held on the number I issue that "(W)hile Rep.
